title: Chapter 67: Vespera Comes North, Part 2 of 5: The Turnip Cart
html:
It was the children who saw it first.
The sun was at its highest, low in the south, and the camp had gone quiet for the middle of the day. Corin was still on the log. Lyra had gone to help with the water skins. And from the south edge of the camp, where the thorn slope came down, there was a sudden shrill shouting, and a clatter of feet, and a small boy came running between the tents with his spear held up over his head, yelling one word over and over in the round Ashborn speech.
Corin did not know the word. But he knew the sound of it. It was the sound a child makes when something is coming.
The hum in his throat stopped.
He got up. It took him a moment, with the crutch. By the time he was on his feet, half the camp was moving. Men were coming out of the tents with bone spears. Women were snatching up babies. Oren came round the side of the bread racks at a run, his sword already out, his face set hard. And Kestrel was walking, not running, from the gray tent toward the south edge of the camp, tall and straight, with Arran a step behind her.
Corin went after them.
The south edge of the camp was crowded with people by the time he got there, all looking up the long slope of the thorns toward the Lip. He pushed between them. Somebody saw his gray hands and moved aside, and then others did, and he came out at the front, beside Oren, on the little gravel shelf between the two thorn bushes where Lyra had stood the day before and faced south.
And he saw it.
It was a cart.
A small one. A farm cart, two-wheeled, with high slatted sides, the kind that takes vegetables to market. It was coming down the goat path through the thorns, very slowly, lurching and bumping and swaying on the loose gravel, with one wheel always higher than the other. It was being pulled by a pony.
The pony was the saddest animal Corin had ever seen. It was small and brown and shaggy, with a long winter coat matted with mud to the belly, and a mane full of burrs, and its head hanging so low that its nose almost touched the path. It walked as if every step might be its last. Behind it the cart creaked and rattled and lurched, and the high slatted sides swayed, and something inside the cart thumped and rolled with every bump.
And beside the pony, holding its bridle, half leading it and half being dragged by it, there was a man.
He was thin. That was the first thing. Thin like a stick, in a long brown coat that was much too big for him and flapped round his knees. He had a red woolen cap pulled down over his ears and a red woolen scarf wound round and round his neck up to his nose. And he was talking. Corin could see it from here. Even at this distance, even through the scarf, the man's mouth was going, and his free hand was waving, and his head kept jerking round to look behind him, up the slope, toward the Lip, every few steps, the way a bird keeps looking round when it is eating on open ground.
"Who's that?" said Oren, very low.
"I don't know," said Corin.
And then the wind changed, a little, and came down the slope toward them through the thorns, and brought the man's voice with it.
"...and I said to her, I said, I'm not going down there, not for any money, not for twice the money, they eat people down there, everybody knows they eat people, and she said, Garrett, she said, if you don't drive this cart down that hill I'll ink your eyelids shut while you sleep, and I said..."
Oren's sword came down, slowly, until the point was resting on the gravel.
"...and I said, you wouldn't, and she said, try me, and so here I am, aren't I, here I am, driving a cart full of turnips down a hill to a camp full of cannibals, at my time of life, with a pony that's going to die on me any minute, look at him, poor beast, he's going to die, I can see it in his eye..."
The pony lifted its head, a little, and looked at the crowd of Ashborn at the bottom of the slope, and the spears, and the smoke, and stopped. And stood there. And would not go on.
"Oh, Saints," said the man. "Oh, Saints, now he's stopped. Come on. Come on, you. They don't eat ponies. Probably. Come on."
The pony did not move.
The man looked at the pony. Then down the slope at the crowd. At the spears and the gray-lined faces and the silent watching children. He seemed to see them properly for the first time. He went very still.
Then he pulled the red scarf down off his face with one shaking hand, and Corin saw a narrow, freckled, frightened face, very young, with a sharp nose and pale eyelashes and a mouth that did not seem to be able to keep shut.
"Hello," the man called down the slope. His voice cracked. "Good afternoon. Is this Last Thorn? I've got a delivery. Turnips. For..." He stopped, and looked behind him at the cart, as if it might tell him. Then back down the slope. And his eyes went along the crowd, quickly, frightened, from face to face. Until they came to Corin's hands.
And stopped there.
And something in the frightened freckled face eased, a little, all at once.
"Oh, thank the Saints," said the man. "Gray hands. You're him. You're the harvester. She said you'd have gray hands. She said look for the gray hands and you'll know you're in the right place." He let go of the pony's bridle and wiped his face with both hands, under the red cap. "Thank the Saints. Two days. Two days on the road. I thought I'd got the wrong camp. I thought I'd got the wrong mountain."
"Who said?" said Corin.
But he thought he knew.
He thought he had known since the words ink your eyelids shut came down the slope on the wind.
The man did not answer. He had turned round and gone to the back of the cart, and he was pulling at something there. A tailboard, held up with two iron pins. He pulled one pin out, and then the other, and the tailboard fell down with a bang, and out of the back of the cart there rolled, bouncing and thumping down the gravel slope toward the crowd, a great many turnips.
They came down through the thorns like a slow brown avalanche. Big ones and small ones, round and knobbly, white and purple, with the dirt still on them. More than he could feel. They bounced off rocks and rolled under bushes and came to rest against the feet of the Ashborn at the bottom, and the children shrieked and scattered and then came back and began, at once, to pick them up.
The man did not watch them. He was climbing up into the back of the cart, scrambling, his long brown coat catching on the slats. And he was kneeling down in the bottom of it, among the last of the turnips, and feeling along the boards with his fingers.
"Hang on," he called. "Hang on. There's a catch. There's a catch here somewhere. She'll kill me if I can't find the catch."
The False Floor
He found the catch.
Corin heard it from the bottom of the slope. A small sharp click, like a key turning in a box. Then a long wooden groan. And the bottom of the cart, the whole floor of it, the boards the turnips had been lying on, lifted up at one end like the lid of a chest.
The man in the red cap heaved it up and over and let it fall back against the slatted side with a crash.
Under it there was a space.
Corin could not see into it from where he stood. But he could see how shallow it was, from the height of the cart's sides. A hand's depth, perhaps. Two hands. Not more. A long flat box, hidden under the false floor, the length of the cart and no deeper than a drawer.
Something moved in it.
A hand came up out of it. Small. Thin. Gray-skinned and wrinkled, with short square-cut nails. And blue. Blue to the wrist, a deep dark stained blue, as if it had been dipped in ink and left to dry, and the blue had gone into the creases of the knuckles and the lines of the palm and under the nails and stayed there.
The hand took hold of the edge of the cart's side. Gripped it. Hard.
Then another hand came up and took hold beside it.
And slowly, with a great deal of grunting and a sound of joints cracking, and a word that Corin did not think the Ashborn children should have heard, a woman sat up out of the bottom of the cart.
She was small and old and gray. Gray hair, cut short and ragged, as if she had cut it herself with a knife and no mirror. A gray face, thin, all lines and bones, with a long sharp nose and a mouth like a slit in a purse. And she was furious. Corin could see it from the bottom of the slope. It came off her like heat off a stove.
There was straw in her hair. There was a piece of turnip leaf stuck to her cheek. Her coat, a long dark coat of some heavy stuff, was crushed and creased all down one side, the side she had been lying on. Round her waist, over the coat, there was a belt made of plain rope, knotted, and hanging from the rope there were things. A great many small things, all along it, on loops of string. Needles. Long ones and short ones, fine ones and thick ones, silver and steel and bone, each in its own little leather sleeve. Little stoppered bottles. A small pair of scissors in the shape of a bird. They clinked when she moved.
She sat there in the bottom of the cart, among the last few turnips, and looked round her. At the thorns. At the slope. At the crowd of Ashborn at the bottom, staring up at her with their spears. At the tents and the smoke. At the milky light in the sky over the ridge beyond.
Then she looked at the man in the red cap.
He had backed away from her into the far corner of the cart, against the slats, as far as he could get. He was holding his cap in both hands in front of his chest.
"Two days," said the woman.
Her voice was low and dry and very clear, and it carried all the way down the slope.
"Two days, Garrett. Two days and two nights. In a box. Under the turnips. With the cart going over every stone between the city and the end of the world, and you singing."
"I had to sing," said the man in the red cap. "There were men at the toll. On the north road. In gray. If I'd stopped singing they'd have wondered why."
"You sang the same song for two days, Garrett."
"It's the only one I know all the words to."
The woman shut her eyes. She sat with them shut for a moment, breathing. Then she opened them again.
"Never again," she said. "Do you hear me? Never again. I don't care if the Archon himself is standing at my door with a hot iron. I don't care if the whole city's on fire. I am never, as long as I live, getting into a box of turnips again."
"No, Mistress Vespera," said Garrett.
"Help me up."
He came, quickly, and took her arm, and she got up. Slowly. She was stiff all over. Corin could see it from the bottom of the slope. Her knees would not straighten at first, and she stood bent over in the cart with one hand on Garrett's shoulder and one hand pressed into the small of her back, and said the word again, quietly. Then she straightened, a little at a time, until she was standing upright in the cart, small and gray and blue-handed and furious, with the straw in her hair and the turnip leaf on her cheek and the needles clinking on her rope belt.
And she looked down the slope, over the heads of the Ashborn, straight at Corin.
He knew her.
He knew her the way you know a coat that has hung by your door for years. The arch under the Dye-Works, with the needles hanging on their rope and the door laid flat on trestles for a table, covered in little pots of ink. The gold-rimmed blue pot. The smell of her shop, wet stone and burnt honey and something sharp, like vinegar. Her blue hands on his face, painting it into somebody else's. Sit. Still. Breathe. He knew all that.
But there were holes in it.
He found them as he looked at her. Places where the memory went smooth and blank, like a page with the words scraped off. A night in her shop he knew had happened, because it was in the Ledger, and he could not see. A rule she had laid down on her floor, that he knew was called rule one, and could not hear her say. Every place where someone else had been in the room with them. Someone who had stood beside him, close, while Vespera worked. Those places were gone. He had burned them. On his knees, under the dome, with the sky coming down. He had burned every one.
He knew who that someone was. He did not have to turn his head. She was standing somewhere behind him in the crowd with the water skins.
She looked at him for a long time across the heads of the crowd.
Then she said, in the same low dry carrying voice, "Harvester. You look terrible."
"So do you," said Corin.
He had not meant to say it. It came out on its own.
The woman in the cart went quite still. Garrett, beside her, made a small frightened noise.
And then the slit of her mouth moved. At one corner. Just a little.
"Well," she said. "You've still got your manners, then. That's something." She brushed the turnip leaf off her cheek with one blue hand. "Somebody get me down off this cart before I fall off it. And somebody give that pony some water before it dies of shame. And then somebody find me Kestrel, because if she's not here, I've come a very long way in a box for nothing."
Nobody moved.
Then, from beside Corin, a voice said quietly, "We are here."
And Kestrel walked out of the crowd, and up the slope, through the scattered turnips, toward the cart.
Old Friends
Kestrel stopped at the side of the cart.
Vespera looked down at her from the cart's bed. Kestrel looked up. Neither of them said anything. The whole slope had gone quiet. The children had stopped picking up turnips. Garrett had stopped breathing, Corin thought, or near enough.
Then Vespera put out her two blue hands.
Not to be helped down. Not like that. She put them out with the forearms turned up, the palms open, the wrists bare where the sleeves of her crushed coat fell back.
And Kestrel reached up and took them. Not by the hands. By the forearms. Her long brown fingers closed round Vespera's thin gray-blue arms, just below the elbows, and Vespera's small blue hands closed round Kestrel's, the same. And they held on. Like that. Arm to arm. The way soldiers grip each other at the end of a long war, or sailors at the end of a long voyage.
They held on for a long time.
Nobody spoke. The pony shifted its feet and blew out through its nose. Somewhere in the camp behind them a goat bell clunked.
"You got old," said Kestrel at last.
"You got tall," said Vespera.
"We were always tall."
"Taller, then." Vespera's eyes were going over Kestrel's face. Over the gray line on the shaved skull, from the nape to the tip of the nose. Slowly. As if she were counting something. "And grayer. Look at you. You were a girl with a painted stripe and a cold in her nose. Now look." Her voice had changed. Gone lower. "How many?"
"Too many to count," said Kestrel. "And one this morning."
Vespera's grip on her arms tightened. Corin saw it.
"Who?"
"Grandfather."
Vespera shut her eyes.
She stood there in the bed of the turnip cart, with her hands round Kestrel's forearms and her eyes shut, and something went across her thin gray face. Corin could not see what it was. It was gone too quickly. But when she opened her eyes again, they were wet.
"Hask," she said. "Old Hask. Saints. I thought he'd see us all out."
"He nearly did."
"How?"
Kestrel did not answer at once. She looked past Vespera's shoulder, down the slope, at Corin. Just for a moment. Then back.
"He took a death that was not his," she said. "To make a man lighter. A man who was carrying too much."
Vespera turned her head and looked at Corin too.
She looked at him for a long time. And he stood there at the bottom of the slope among the Ashborn, leaning on his crutch, and let her look.
"Of course he did," said Vespera at last, very quietly. "Of course. The old fool." And then, still more quietly, so that Corin hardly heard it: "Good."
She let go of Kestrel's arms.
And Kestrel reached up and took her by the waist, the way you lift a child down from a wagon, and lifted her down out of the cart, easily, and set her on her feet on the gravel. Vespera staggered. Her stiff knees nearly gave. Kestrel held her until they did not.
"Put me down, I'm not a parcel," said Vespera.
"You came in a box," said Kestrel.
And Vespera laughed.
It was the first time Corin had ever heard her laugh. He was sure of it, holes or no holes. It came out of her short and hoarse and surprised, like a door that has not been opened in years creaking on its hinges. And her face changed when she did it. All of it. The slit of a mouth opened and went up at both corners, all the way, and the lines round her eyes folded up, and for a moment the small furious gray woman from under the Dye-Works looked like someone quite different. Someone younger. Someone who had sat by a fire at Last Thorn many years ago, with a cold in her nose, and laughed at a tall girl with a painted stripe.
Corin had never seen her smile all the way before. He was sure of that too.
Then it was gone, and she was brushing the straw out of her short gray hair and scowling.
"You knew each other," he said. It came out stupidly. He did not know what else to say.
Vespera looked at him over Kestrel's arm.
"I came north once," she said. "Years ago. More years than I'm going to tell you, harvester. When I was young and knew everything." She sniffed. "I'd heard about them. The people at the edge who carried their dead together. I wanted to see how it was done. So I'd know how to ink people who couldn't."
"Couldn't what?"
"Carry." She held up one blue hand. "People like you. People who'd taken too much and had nobody to share it with. People who were drowning. I thought, if I could see how the Ashborn did it, I could learn to do it with a needle. Put a line in them. A rail to hold on to." She dropped the hand. "I stayed a winter. Old Hask taught me. And this one," she jerked her chin at Kestrel, "followed me round like a lost goat the whole time asking what every needle was for."
"You let us," said Kestrel.
"I let you. Saints help me." Vespera looked up at the tall woman, and the corner of her mouth went up again. Not all the way, this time. But nearly. "You were the only one who ever listened."
Garrett had climbed down from the cart on the other side. He stood holding the drooping pony's bridle and looked from one woman to the other, and then at the crowd of silent Ashborn with their spears, and then, nervously, back over his shoulder at the slope behind him, up toward the Lip.
"Is anybody going to eat me?" he said. "Only I'd like to know. Before I sit down."
Nobody answered him. But a small Ashborn girl came up the slope, solemnly, through the turnips, and took the pony's bridle out of his hand, and led it away toward the water.
